labs.title: Storytelling & Slide Decks with AI
labs.cardSummary: One XBeton story told three ways: ten-card Gamma decks for homeowners, builders and specifiers, with a recorded walkthrough in my own voice.

hero.b: Three decks that each answer a different question.

labs.lede: XBeton sells an AAC (autoclaved aerated concrete) building system. Homeowners, builders and architects all ask different questions about it, so one generic deck would not work for any of them. I built a separate ten-card deck for each audience in Gamma, kept one brand and one evidence register across all three, and recorded a walkthrough explaining the choices.
facts:
XBeton, AAC blocks and panels
Real company marketing need

Gamma, Claude and Codex
Generation, refinement, Freeform edits

video.title: My walkthrough
video.meta: 3 min 50 s · recorded in my own voice
video.caption: Submitted to MasterClass as my lab deliverable. Recorded in my own voice with the finished decks on screen.

approach: Split the audience first. Homeowners care about comfort and design, builders about scope and crew planning, specifiers about evidence and assembly detail. Each deck opens with that audience's question and closes on its own next step.

One evidence register for all three decks. Every quantified claim was checked against the source documents. The six-hour fire rating conflicts with the 2025 FAQ (four hours), so it stays visibly marked [NEEDS VERIFY] on every deck that mentions it.

AI drafted, I directed. Gamma generated the first versions from detailed briefs. Sixteen rounds of saved prompts then fixed the theme, logo, image sharpness and labels, and I finished placement in Freeform.
Built to reuse. The brand system, prompts and module plan are portable. Swap the brand variables, evidence and calls to action to build a new client's decks.

labs.title: Data & Financial Analysis & Dashboards with AI
labs.cardSummary: A Q4 decision dashboard for a fictional DTC brand: 10,800 orders reconciled, nine scenarios, and a recommendation I changed when the numbers pushed back.

hero.a: More orders didn't mean more profit.

labs.lede: Button & Bear, a fictional online teddy-bear business, had to pick its Q4 offer: keep the promotion, reset prices and shipping, or launch a bundle. I used AI to reconcile the data, model nine scenarios and stress-test the answer. The bundle looked best on profit alone, but its lead disappeared once customers could switch to it, so I recommended piloting the reset first.
facts:
Button & Bear, fictional DTC
Q4 offer decision

Interactive dashboard
plus a 10-sheet working model

video.title: My presentation
video.meta: 4 min 22 s · recorded in my own voice
video.caption: An executive walkthrough of the decision, the verified findings and the recommendation, recorded over the finished dashboard.

approach: Check the data before trusting it. Every order and item line was audited and reconciled to the monthly records. Shipping was calculated per order, not per line, so it was not counted twice. The original workbooks stayed unchanged.
Explain the gap. Q3 orders beat budget by 20%, yet operating profit was about $5,500 against a $31,400 plan. Discounts removed about $21,000 and higher shipping cost per order another $9,000.

Challenge the first answer. In the base case the bundle led the reset by only about $2,200. When customers who planned to buy both bears switched to the cheaper bundle, its profit fell below the reset.
Recommend a pilot, not a leap. Pilot the price and shipping reset, track contribution per visitor, then test the bundle against it with limited stock exposure.
